rules.note: A Can-Do is mastered after 3 successful demonstrations (score 80+, confirmed by Triple-Layer feedback) in different speaking or writing tasks at the active sub-band. When every Can-Do of the active sub-band is mastered, the learner moves to the next sub-band.

levels.name: Beginner
levels.summary: Introducing yourself, basic needs, daily routines and your immediate surroundings.

sub_bands.goal: Can introduce themselves and express basic needs.

grammar_targets.title: Verb 'be' (am / is / are)
grammar_targets.explanation: Use 'be' to say who you are, your age and where you're from; add 'not' for negatives and swap the order for questions.
grammar_targets.example: I am Mehmet. I'm 30. Are you a teacher? No, I'm not.

grammar_targets.title: Subject pronouns and possessive adjectives
grammar_targets.explanation: Learn I/you/he/she/it/we/they and my/your/his/her/our/their; English splits 'he', 'she' and 'it'.
grammar_targets.example: This is my sister. Her name is Elif. She lives in Izmir.

grammar_targets.title: a / an and regular plurals
grammar_targets.explanation: Use a/an before jobs and singular countable nouns; add -s to make most nouns plural.
grammar_targets.example: I'm an engineer. I have two brothers and a dog.

grammar_targets.title: Question words: what, where, how old, how
grammar_targets.explanation: Ask for personal information: What's your name? Where are you from? How old are you?
grammar_targets.example: Where are you from? I'm from Turkey.

items.meaning: the name before your family name
items.example: My first name is Mehmet.
How do you spell your surname?

items.meaning: to come from a country or city
items.example: I'm from Istanbul.

items.meaning: to have your home in a place
items.example: I live in Ankara.
She is married with two children.

items.meaning: the work you do for money
items.example: What's your job? I'm a nurse.

items.meaning: a polite way to say 'I want'
items.example: I'd like a coffee, please.

items.meaning: a polite way to ask for something
items.example: Can I have some water, please?

items.meaning: a polite way to get attention
items.example: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
How much is this sandwich?

items.meaning: to make something easier for someone
items.example: Can you help me, please?

items.meaning: words to show you are grateful
items.example: Thank you very much!

can_do_statements.text: Can introduce themselves and answer simple questions about name, age, nationality and where they live.
Can ask for basic things such as food, drinks or the toilet using simple polite phrases.
Can write a short, simple self-introduction with name, age, country and job.
Can fill in a simple form or note with personal details.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I have 30 years.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I am 30 (years old).
l1_interference_alerts.note: Age uses 'be', not 'have' (Turkish expresses age with a possessive form).

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I teacher.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I am a teacher.
l1_interference_alerts.note: English needs the verb 'am' where Turkish uses the suffix '-im', so don't drop it.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: My sister, he is a doctor.
l1_interference_alerts.right: My sister is a doctor. She ...
l1_interference_alerts.note: Turkish 'o' has no gender; English uses he (male), she (female) and it (things).

speaking_scenarios.title: Hotel check-in
speaking_scenarios.setting: You arrive at a small hotel in London. The receptionist asks for your details.
speaking_scenarios.task: Say hello, give your name, spell your surname, say where you are from and ask for the Wi-Fi password.

speaking_scenarios.title: A new classmate
speaking_scenarios.setting: It is the first day of an English course. A classmate starts talking to you.
speaking_scenarios.task: Introduce yourself: name, age, city, job and one thing about your family. Ask two questions back.

speaking_scenarios.title: Language school registration
speaking_scenarios.setting: A secretary fills in your registration form at a language school.
speaking_scenarios.task: Answer questions about your name, address, phone number, nationality and job.

sub_bands.goal: Can describe daily routines and their immediate surroundings in simple terms.

grammar_targets.title: Present simple and 3rd person -s
grammar_targets.explanation: Use the present simple for habits; add -s to the verb after he/she/it (works, goes, has).
grammar_targets.example: I get up at 7. My brother works in a bank.

grammar_targets.title: Adverbs of frequency
grammar_targets.explanation: Put always, usually, often, sometimes and never before the main verb but after 'be'.
grammar_targets.example: I usually walk to work. I'm never late.

grammar_targets.title: There is / there are + prepositions of place
grammar_targets.explanation: Say what is in a place with there is/are plus in, on, under, next to, opposite or between.
grammar_targets.example: There's a café next to the bank. There are two chairs in the kitchen.

grammar_targets.title: can / can't for ability
grammar_targets.explanation: Use can + base verb for ability, with no 'to' after can.
grammar_targets.example: I can swim, but I can't drive.

items.meaning: to leave your bed in the morning
items.example: I get up at seven.

items.meaning: to eat the first meal of the day
items.example: We have breakfast at home.
She goes to work by bus.

items.meaning: to wash your body under running water
items.example: I take a shower every morning.

items.meaning: to stop working for the day
items.example: I finish work at six.

items.meaning: to lie down to sleep at night
items.example: I usually go to bed at eleven.

items.meaning: very close to, at the side of
items.example: The café is next to the park.
The bank is opposite the station.

items.meaning: the place where a bus stops
items.example: There's a bus stop near my house.
My neighbourhood is quiet.

items.meaning: the main room for relaxing at home
items.example: We watch TV in the living room.

items.meaning: a large shop for food and household things
items.example: I go to the supermarket on Saturdays.

can_do_statements.text: Can describe their daily routine and habits in simple sentences.
Can ask and answer where places are in a town using simple prepositions.
Can write a short message about their day, home and habits.
Can say what they like and dislike with a simple reason.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: She work in a hospital.
l1_interference_alerts.right: She works in a hospital.
l1_interference_alerts.note: In the present simple, the verb takes -s after he/she/it.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I make my homework.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I do my homework.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Turkish 'yapmak' covers both 'do' and 'make': do homework, make a cake.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I go to home.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I go home.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Don't use 'to' before 'home'.

speaking_scenarios.title: My weekday
speaking_scenarios.setting: A new friend asks what a normal weekday looks like for you.
speaking_scenarios.task: Describe your day from morning to night with times and at least two frequency adverbs.

speaking_scenarios.title: Directions in a new town
speaking_scenarios.setting: You are lost in a small town and ask a local for help.
speaking_scenarios.task: Ask where the bank, the station and a café are, and repeat the directions back.

speaking_scenarios.title: Flatmate interview
speaking_scenarios.setting: You want to share a flat. The owner asks about your habits.
speaking_scenarios.task: Talk about when you get up, what you can cook and what you like doing at home.

levels.name: Elementary
levels.summary: Past events, simple shopping and transactions, plans and comparisons.

sub_bands.goal: Can talk about past events and handle simple everyday transactions.

grammar_targets.title: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
grammar_targets.explanation: Use the past simple for finished events (worked, went, saw); use 'did' + base verb in negatives and questions.
grammar_targets.example: Last weekend I went to Bursa. We didn't stay long.

grammar_targets.title: Past of 'be': was / were
grammar_targets.explanation: Use 'was' with I/he/she/it and 'were' with you/we/they.
grammar_targets.example: The hotel was nice but the rooms were small.

grammar_targets.title: Countable / uncountable: some, any, much, many
grammar_targets.explanation: Information, advice and money are uncountable, so they never take a plural -s.
grammar_targets.example: Can I have some information? How many tickets do you need?

grammar_targets.title: Polite requests: Could I...? / I'd like...
grammar_targets.explanation: Ask politely with could, would like and please.
grammar_targets.example: Could I have a return ticket to Oxford, please?

items.meaning: a paper that shows what you paid
items.example: Can I have the receipt, please?

items.meaning: money you get back after paying
items.example: Here's your change.
Is there a student discount?

items.meaning: to put clothes on to check the fit
items.example: Can I try on this jacket?

items.meaning: money given back for a returned item
items.example: I'd like a refund, please.
These shoes are on sale.
A return ticket to York, please.

items.meaning: where you get on a train
items.example: The train leaves from platform 4.

items.meaning: a time when something is late
items.example: There's a twenty-minute delay.
I booked a room online.

items.meaning: to register at a hotel or airport
items.example: We checked in at three.
My luggage didn't arrive.

can_do_statements.text: Can handle simple transactions in shops, cafés, hotels and stations.
Can tell a simple story about a past weekend, trip or event.
Can write a short email to a friend describing a past event.
Can write a simple request, booking or order message.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I didn't went.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I didn't go.
l1_interference_alerts.note: After 'did', keep the base verb; 'did' already shows the past.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: Yesterday I go to the cinema.
l1_interference_alerts.right: Yesterday I went to the cinema.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Turkish can rely on context, but English verbs must change for past time.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: Can you give me some informations?
l1_interference_alerts.right: Can you give me some information?
l1_interference_alerts.note: Information, advice and furniture are uncountable and never take -s.

speaking_scenarios.title: At the train station
speaking_scenarios.setting: You need a ticket to Cambridge for tomorrow morning.
speaking_scenarios.task: Ask for a return ticket, the price, the platform and whether there are delays.

speaking_scenarios.title: My last holiday
speaking_scenarios.setting: A colleague asks about your last holiday.
speaking_scenarios.task: Tell the story: where you went, who with, what you did and one problem that happened.

speaking_scenarios.title: Returning a faulty item
speaking_scenarios.setting: The headphones you bought last week stopped working.
speaking_scenarios.task: Explain the problem, show the receipt and ask for a refund or a new pair.

sub_bands.goal: Can describe plans, make basic comparisons and give simple directions.

grammar_targets.title: Future: be going to and present continuous for arrangements
grammar_targets.explanation: Use 'going to' for plans and intentions, and the present continuous for fixed arrangements.
grammar_targets.example: I'm going to learn to drive. I'm meeting Ali on Friday.

grammar_targets.title: Comparatives and superlatives
grammar_targets.explanation: Add -er/-est to short adjectives and use more/most with long ones, but never both together.
grammar_targets.example: Izmir is warmer than Ankara. It's the most beautiful city I know.

grammar_targets.title: Imperatives for directions and instructions
grammar_targets.explanation: Start directions with the verb: Turn left, Go straight on, Take the second right.
grammar_targets.example: Go straight on, then turn right at the traffic lights.

grammar_targets.title: Present continuous vs present simple
grammar_targets.explanation: Use the continuous for what is happening now and the simple form for habits.
grammar_targets.example: I usually drive, but today I'm taking the bus.

items.meaning: to decide what you will do
items.example: Let's make plans for the weekend.
Are you free on Saturday?

items.meaning: to ask someone to come to an event
items.example: She invited me to her party.

items.meaning: to say no to an offer
items.example: I had to turn down the invitation.
We arranged to meet at eight.

items.meaning: a way to make a suggestion
items.example: How about going to the cinema?
The market is always crowded.
The village is very peaceful.
Kadıköy is a lively area.
The people are really friendly.
London is more expensive than Istanbul.
The hotel is in a convenient location.

can_do_statements.text: Can make, accept and decline invitations and simple arrangements.
Can give and follow simple directions.
Can compare two places, products or options with simple reasons.
Can write about future plans for a holiday, weekend or the coming year.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: It is more cheaper.
l1_interference_alerts.right: It is cheaper.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Don't use -er and 'more' together.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I am agree with you.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I agree with you.
l1_interference_alerts.note: 'Agree' is a verb, so it doesn't need 'am' in front of it.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: Turn the right.
l1_interference_alerts.right: Turn right.
l1_interference_alerts.note: No 'the' before 'right' or 'left' in directions.

speaking_scenarios.title: Planning the weekend
speaking_scenarios.setting: A friend calls to make plans for Saturday.
speaking_scenarios.task: Suggest two activities, decline one politely, agree a time and a place to meet.

speaking_scenarios.title: Helping a tourist
speaking_scenarios.setting: A tourist asks you how to get to the museum from the main square.
speaking_scenarios.task: Give clear directions with at least three imperatives and one landmark.

speaking_scenarios.title: Two cities
speaking_scenarios.setting: A friend from abroad asks which city to visit in Turkey.
speaking_scenarios.task: Compare two cities you know: weather, prices, people and things to do. Recommend one.

levels.name: Intermediate
levels.summary: Giving opinions, describing experiences, hypothetical situations and work emails.

sub_bands.goal: Can give and explain opinions on familiar topics.

grammar_targets.title: Present perfect vs past simple
grammar_targets.explanation: Use the past simple for finished events at a stated time, and the present perfect for life experience and present results.
grammar_targets.example: I've been to Rome twice. I went there last May.

grammar_targets.title: Present perfect with for / since / just / already / yet
grammar_targets.explanation: For situations continuing until now, use 'since' with a starting point and 'for' with a length of time.
grammar_targets.example: I've worked here since 2020. I haven't finished yet.

grammar_targets.title: Linking ideas: although, however, because of, so
grammar_targets.explanation: Link ideas: put 'however' at the start of a sentence with a comma, and 'although' inside a sentence.
grammar_targets.example: Although the job is stressful, I enjoy it. However, the pay is low.

grammar_targets.title: Opinion language
grammar_targets.explanation: Introduce your view with phrases like In my opinion, I think that or As far as I'm concerned.
grammar_targets.example: In my opinion, working from home saves time.

items.example: I see your point, but I disagree.
On the other hand, it's very expensive.

items.meaning: I don't fully believe it yet
items.example: I'm not convinced it's a good idea.
That's a fair point about the cost.
To be honest, I prefer the old version.
It depends on the weather.

items.meaning: the last day to finish something
items.example: The deadline is Friday.
My colleagues are very supportive.

items.meaning: to formally ask for a job or place
items.example: I applied for a new job.

items.meaning: to have the duty to manage something
items.example: I'm responsible for the budget.
I want to gain experience abroad.

items.meaning: time split well between work and life
items.example: A good work-life balance matters to me.

can_do_statements.text: Can give and briefly justify opinions and plans on familiar topics.
Can describe experiences, events, hopes and ambitions.
Can write a short opinion paragraph with reasons and examples.
Can write a personal letter describing experiences and feelings.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I am living here since 2019.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I have lived (been living) here since 2019.
l1_interference_alerts.note: With 'since' and 'for' for situations continuing to now, use the present perfect.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: It depends to the price.
l1_interference_alerts.right: It depends on the price.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Turkish uses a dative ending here, but English says 'depend on'.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I'm interested about history.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I'm interested in history.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Learn prepositions as fixed phrases: interested in, good at, afraid of.

speaking_scenarios.title: First job interview
speaking_scenarios.setting: You are interviewed for a junior position in a company you like.
speaking_scenarios.task: Talk about your experience, one achievement and why you want the job. Use present perfect at least twice.

speaking_scenarios.title: Social media debate
speaking_scenarios.setting: Friends discuss whether social media is good for teenagers.
speaking_scenarios.task: Give your opinion with two reasons, react to the opposite view and conclude.

speaking_scenarios.title: A life experience
speaking_scenarios.setting: A new friend asks about the most interesting thing you have ever done.
speaking_scenarios.task: Describe the experience, how you felt and what you learned from it.

sub_bands.goal: Can handle hypothetical situations and write everyday professional emails.

grammar_targets.title: First and second conditional
grammar_targets.explanation: Real possibility: If + present, will. Imaginary situation: If + past, would. Never put 'would' in the if-clause.
grammar_targets.example: If it rains, we'll stay in. If I had more time, I would travel more.

grammar_targets.title: Passive voice (present and past)
grammar_targets.explanation: Focus on the action rather than who did it: be + past participle.
grammar_targets.example: The report was sent yesterday. Breakfast is served at eight.

grammar_targets.title: Relative clauses: who, which, that, where
grammar_targets.explanation: Define nouns with who for people, which/that for things and where for places.
grammar_targets.example: The colleague who helped me is from Spain.

grammar_targets.title: Reported speech (statements and requests)
grammar_targets.explanation: When reporting, move the tense one step back: 'I'm tired' becomes She said she was tired.
grammar_targets.example: He told me that the meeting had been cancelled.

items.meaning: opening phrase stating an email's purpose
items.example: I'm writing to ask about the invoice.
Regarding your last email, ...

items.meaning: the file is included with this email
items.example: Please find attached the updated plan.
I'm following up on our call.

items.word: look forward to hearing from you
items.meaning: formal email closing hoping for a reply
items.example: I look forward to hearing from you.
Please reply at your earliest convenience.

items.meaning: to take action to handle something
items.example: I'll deal with the problem today.

items.meaning: to fix or organize a problem
items.example: We need to sort out the booking.
She came up with a great idea.
We've run out of paper.
I can't figure out how it works.

items.meaning: to formally say you are unhappy
items.example: I'd like to make a complaint.

can_do_statements.text: Can discuss hypothetical situations and their consequences.
Can deal with most situations while travelling, including making a complaint.
Can write a clear professional email making a request or a complaint.
Can write a short report on a familiar topic giving advantages and disadvantages.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: If I would have money, I would buy a car.
l1_interference_alerts.right: If I had money, I would buy a car.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Never use 'would' in the if-clause.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: Can you explain me the problem?
l1_interference_alerts.right: Can you explain the problem to me?
l1_interference_alerts.note: Use explain/describe + thing + to + person.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I'm waiting your answer.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I look forward to hearing from you.
l1_interference_alerts.note: 'Wait' needs 'for', and formal emails use the fixed phrase 'I look forward to hearing from you'.

speaking_scenarios.title: Hotel complaint
speaking_scenarios.setting: Your hotel room is noisy and the air conditioning is broken.
speaking_scenarios.task: Complain politely at reception, explain the problems and negotiate a solution.

speaking_scenarios.title: Delay update to a client
speaking_scenarios.setting: A project you manage will be one week late.
speaking_scenarios.task: Explain the reason, what has been done and propose a new date. Use the passive at least once.

speaking_scenarios.title: If you won the lottery
speaking_scenarios.setting: Friends imagine winning a big prize.
speaking_scenarios.task: Say what you would do, what you wouldn't change and why.

levels.name: Upper-Intermediate
levels.summary: Building coherent arguments, weighing pros and cons, speculating about the past and shifting register.

sub_bands.goal: Can build a clear argument and weigh pros and cons.

grammar_targets.title: Contrast and concession: despite, whereas, even though
grammar_targets.explanation: Use despite/in spite of + noun or -ing, even though + clause, and whereas to contrast two situations.
grammar_targets.example: Despite the cost, the plan makes sense. Even though it's risky, it's worth trying.

grammar_targets.title: Modals of speculation (present)
grammar_targets.explanation: Use must (almost certain), might/could (possible) and can't (impossible) + verb to speculate about now.
grammar_targets.example: She must be busy; she can't be at home.

grammar_targets.title: Narrative tenses: past continuous and past perfect
grammar_targets.explanation: Use the past continuous for background action and the past perfect for an earlier event.
grammar_targets.example: I was driving home when I realised I had left my phone at work.

grammar_targets.title: Gerund vs infinitive with meaning change
grammar_targets.explanation: Some verbs change meaning: stop doing vs stop to do, remember doing vs remember to do.
grammar_targets.example: I stopped smoking. I stopped to buy a coffee.

items.meaning: to bring a topic up for discussion
items.example: I'd like to raise an issue about safety.

items.meaning: a very important cause or element
items.example: Price is a key factor.
The benefits outweigh the risks.
On balance, I support the idea.
We should take costs into account.
The main drawback is the noise.
They use cutting-edge software.
The app raised privacy concerns.

items.meaning: to depend on someone or something
items.example: We rely too much on our phones.
Automation will change many jobs.
The new design is more user-friendly.
Parents worry about screen time.

can_do_statements.text: Can present a clear argument, weighing advantages and disadvantages of options.
Can take an active part in discussion, accounting for and sustaining their views.
Can write an essay developing an argument with supporting details.
Can write clear, detailed descriptions of real or imaginary events and experiences.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: Despite of the rain, we went out.
l1_interference_alerts.right: Despite the rain, we went out.
l1_interference_alerts.note: 'Despite' takes no preposition; 'in spite of' does take 'of'.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: According to me, it's wrong.
l1_interference_alerts.right: In my view / I'd argue that it's wrong.
l1_interference_alerts.note: 'According to' reports other people's views, not your own.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I want to say my idea.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I'd like to share / put forward my view.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Don't translate the Turkish 'say my idea' word for word; use share, express or put forward.

speaking_scenarios.title: Remote work debate
speaking_scenarios.setting: Your team debates whether to keep working remotely three days a week.
speaking_scenarios.task: Present both sides, give your recommendation and respond to one objection.

speaking_scenarios.title: Scholarship interview
speaking_scenarios.setting: A panel interviews you for a scholarship abroad.
speaking_scenarios.task: Explain your goals, a challenge you overcame and how the scholarship would help.

speaking_scenarios.title: Car-free city centres
speaking_scenarios.setting: A local radio show asks listeners for their opinions.
speaking_scenarios.task: Argue for or against banning cars from the city centre, with evidence and a counter-argument.

sub_bands.goal: Can speculate about the past and switch confidently between formal and informal register.

grammar_targets.title: Third conditional
grammar_targets.explanation: For things that did not happen in the past: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.
grammar_targets.example: If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the flight.

grammar_targets.title: Modals of deduction (past)
grammar_targets.explanation: Draw conclusions about the past with must have, might have or can't have + past participle.
grammar_targets.example: He must have forgotten. She can't have seen the message.

grammar_targets.title: Formal vs informal register
grammar_targets.explanation: In formal style, avoid contractions and phrasal verbs and prefer Latin-based verbs: get becomes obtain, ask for becomes request.
grammar_targets.example: Informal: Can you get back to me? Formal: I would appreciate a reply.

grammar_targets.title: wish / if only
grammar_targets.explanation: Present regret: wish + past simple. Past regret: wish + past perfect.
grammar_targets.example: I wish I spoke Spanish. If only I had studied harder.

items.example: You must obtain a permit first.
I would like to request an extension.
Our staff will assist you.
Please inform us of any changes.
The role requires travel.
The meeting will commence at nine.
In hindsight, it was a mistake.
I didn't want to let the team down.

items.meaning: to feel happy a worry is gone
items.example: I was relieved to hear the news.

items.meaning: to feel sorry about something you did
items.example: I regret not taking the job.
She felt frustrated with the delays.
It's a shame you couldn't come.

can_do_statements.text: Can speculate about causes, consequences and past events.
Can switch between formal and informal register appropriately for the listener.
Can write formal letters and emails, adapting tone to the reader.
Can write a review evaluating a film, book, product or service.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: If I had known, I would come.
l1_interference_alerts.right: If I had known, I would have come.
l1_interference_alerts.note: In past conditionals, the result clause uses 'would have' + past participle.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I want you to send the file.
l1_interference_alerts.right: Could you possibly send the file?
l1_interference_alerts.note: A direct request that sounds natural in Turkish can seem rude in formal English.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I wish I would study more.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I wish I had studied more.
l1_interference_alerts.note: For past regret, use wish + past perfect.

speaking_scenarios.title: Explaining a mistake
speaking_scenarios.setting: A client order went wrong last week and your manager asks what happened.
speaking_scenarios.task: Speculate about the causes with past modals, take responsibility and suggest prevention.

speaking_scenarios.title: Same news, two registers
speaking_scenarios.setting: You got a new job. Tell your best friend, then inform your current manager.
speaking_scenarios.task: Give the news twice: once informally, once formally. Change vocabulary and tone, not facts.

speaking_scenarios.title: A turning point
speaking_scenarios.setting: A podcast host asks about a turning point in your life.
speaking_scenarios.task: Describe it and imagine how things would have been different, using the third conditional.

levels.name: Advanced
levels.summary: Fluent, emphatic expression, idioms, abstract topics and precise control of discourse.

sub_bands.goal: Can express ideas fluently with emphasis, nuance and well-chosen idioms.

grammar_targets.title: Inversion for emphasis
grammar_targets.explanation: After a negative or limiting adverb at the start, use question word order: Never have I..., Not only did..., Rarely do...
grammar_targets.example: Not only did we finish early, but we also cut costs.

grammar_targets.title: Cleft sentences
grammar_targets.explanation: Split a sentence to focus on one part: What I need is..., It was Ali who..., The thing that worries me is...
grammar_targets.example: What really matters is the long-term impact.

grammar_targets.title: Mixed conditionals
grammar_targets.explanation: Link a past condition to a present result, or the reverse: If I had taken that job, I would be in London now.
grammar_targets.example: If I were more patient, I wouldn't have argued with him.

grammar_targets.title: Impersonal passive: It is said that / He is thought to...
grammar_targets.explanation: Report beliefs without naming a source: It is believed that..., She is said to have...
grammar_targets.example: The company is thought to be planning a merger.

items.example: Let's get the ball rolling with a quick update.

items.meaning: a problem that turns out well
items.example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
We need to be on the same page before the launch.

items.meaning: to do something badly to save time
items.example: We can't afford to cut corners on safety.

items.meaning: a small visible part of a bigger problem
items.example: These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.
The new role was a steep learning curve.
It is arguably the best solution we have.
I agree to some extent.
It is by no means a simple task.
It goes without saying that quality comes first.
Admittedly, the first version had problems.
First and foremost, we need funding.

can_do_statements.text: Can express ideas fluently and spontaneously, adding emphasis and nuance.
Can use idiomatic language appropriately in social and professional contexts.
Can write well-structured texts that use emphasis and hedging deliberately.
Can write persuasive proposals for a professional audience.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: It doesn't come from my hand.
l1_interference_alerts.right: There's nothing I can do about it.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Idioms like 'elimden gelmiyor' can't be translated word for word.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I humbly request your kind consideration of my humble proposal.
l1_interference_alerts.right: I would be grateful if you could consider my proposal.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Overly ornate formal phrasing sounds unnatural in English; be clear and polite.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I'm in the opinion that...
l1_interference_alerts.right: I'm of the opinion that...
l1_interference_alerts.note: The fixed phrase is 'of the opinion'.

speaking_scenarios.title: Project pitch
speaking_scenarios.setting: You pitch a new product idea to senior management in five minutes.
speaking_scenarios.task: Open with impact, use one inversion and one cleft sentence, handle a sceptical question.

speaking_scenarios.title: Senior-level interview
speaking_scenarios.setting: A behavioural interview for a team-lead role.
speaking_scenarios.task: Describe a difficult decision you made, what you would do differently and what you learned.

speaking_scenarios.title: A controversial story
speaking_scenarios.setting: Friends discuss a controversial news story over dinner.
speaking_scenarios.task: Give a nuanced view, hedge where you are unsure and use two idioms naturally.

sub_bands.goal: Can argue abstract and complex topics with precise discourse control.

grammar_targets.title: Subjunctive
grammar_targets.explanation: Use the base verb after formal suggestions and requirements: It is essential that he be informed. I suggest she apply.
grammar_targets.example: The board recommended that the policy be reviewed.

grammar_targets.title: Advanced discourse markers
grammar_targets.explanation: Signal precise logical moves with that said, by the same token, notwithstanding, in light of and be that as it may.
grammar_targets.example: The data is limited. That said, the trend is clear.

grammar_targets.title: Participle clauses
grammar_targets.explanation: Replace long 'and... and...' chains with participle clauses: Having finished..., Given that..., Faced with...
grammar_targets.example: Faced with rising costs, the company changed its strategy.

grammar_targets.title: Nominalisation
grammar_targets.explanation: In academic and formal writing, turn verbs into nouns: 'prices rose quickly' becomes 'the rapid rise in prices'.
grammar_targets.example: The rapid growth of remote work has transformed city centres.

items.meaning: a likely consequence or hidden meaning
items.example: The implications of this decision are serious.
We need to address the underlying causes.

items.meaning: a natural, permanent part of something
items.example: Every plan has inherent risks.
Women constitute half of the workforce.
We took steps to mitigate the risk.
AI represents a paradigm shift in education.
Rising sea levels pose a threat to coastal cities.

items.meaning: to show how two things differ
items.example: We should draw a distinction between data and opinion.
The study sheds light on sleep patterns.
Bear in mind that budgets are tight.
She made a compelling case for reform.
It is widely acknowledged that sleep affects memory.

can_do_statements.text: Can argue abstract and complex topics with precise discourse control.
Can lead a discussion, summarising and redirecting contributions.
Can write clear academic or professional texts using nominalisation and cohesion.
Can summarise and synthesise information from several sources.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: We made a research and we found and we saw that...
l1_interference_alerts.right: Having conducted the research, we found that...
l1_interference_alerts.note: Instead of long Turkish-style 'and' chains, use participle clauses and nominalisation.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: make research
l1_interference_alerts.right: do / conduct research
l1_interference_alerts.note: 'Research' is uncountable and goes with do, conduct or carry out.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: This subject is very important for me.
l1_interference_alerts.right: This issue is of particular importance to me.
l1_interference_alerts.note: In academic or formal style, choose more precise phrasing than 'very important for me'.

speaking_scenarios.title: Chairing a tense meeting
speaking_scenarios.setting: Two departments disagree about budget priorities and you chair the meeting.
speaking_scenarios.task: Open the meeting, summarise both positions neutrally, redirect a digression and propose next steps.

speaking_scenarios.title: Academic panel
speaking_scenarios.setting: A panel questions you about a project or idea you know well.
speaking_scenarios.task: Explain its rationale and limitations, using nominalisation and at least one subjunctive.

speaking_scenarios.title: Is technology making us less human?
speaking_scenarios.setting: A philosophical café debate.
speaking_scenarios.task: Argue a position on this abstract question with examples, concessions and a clear conclusion.

levels.name: Mastery
levels.summary: Resolving ambiguity, irony and style, native-like rhetoric and sociolinguistic finesse.

sub_bands.goal: Can resolve ambiguity and use irony and style deliberately.

grammar_targets.title: Fronting and ellipsis for style
grammar_targets.explanation: Move an element to the front and leave out repetition for emphasis and flow: 'Strange though it may seem, ...'
grammar_targets.example: Strange though it may seem, the quieter option sold better.

grammar_targets.title: Fine modal distinctions
grammar_targets.explanation: Distinguish needn't have done (done, but unnecessary) from didn't need to (not necessary), and use might well and would sooner.
grammar_targets.example: You needn't have booked; the restaurant was empty.

grammar_targets.title: Understatement and irony structures
grammar_targets.explanation: Create irony by softening what you say with not exactly, hardly, not the most... and a bit of a.
grammar_targets.example: It wasn't exactly the smoothest launch in history.

grammar_targets.title: Complex noun phrases and apposition
grammar_targets.explanation: Pack information into dense noun phrases and appositives: 'Ayse, a quietly brilliant engineer, ...'
grammar_targets.example: The report, a meticulous two-year study, changed the debate.

items.example: She's frugal, not stingy.
Be assertive without being pushy.
An inquisitive mind asks better questions.
A slender majority voted yes.
Thank you for your candid feedback.
Her research is meticulous.

items.meaning: said as a joke, not seriously
items.example: His comment was tongue-in-cheek.
Calling it 'adequate' was damning with faint praise.
The result was a far cry from what we promised.

items.meaning: of a rough or doubtful kind
items.example: It was a holiday of sorts.

items.meaning: saying it more gently than it is
items.example: The meeting was tense, to put it mildly.
Read between the lines of the announcement.

can_do_statements.text: Can resolve ambiguity and convey finer shades of meaning precisely.
Can use irony and understatement deliberately and recognise them in others.
Can write sophisticated texts with a deliberate and consistent style.
Can write engaging narratives using stylistic devices.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: The hotel was cheap and good. (formal review)
l1_interference_alerts.right: The hotel was inexpensive and excellent value.
l1_interference_alerts.note: 'Cheap' often suggests low quality; manage the connotation.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: I didn't need to bring an umbrella, but I brought it. (meant: unnecessary)
l1_interference_alerts.right: I needn't have brought an umbrella.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Needn't have = you did it but it was unnecessary; didn't need to = it wasn't necessary (whether you did it is unclear).

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: It was very very good.
l1_interference_alerts.right: It was outstanding / remarkable.
l1_interference_alerts.note: Use strong adjectives instead of repeating 'very'.

speaking_scenarios.title: Diplomatic negative feedback
speaking_scenarios.setting: You must tell a valued partner that their work was not good enough.
speaking_scenarios.task: Deliver the message clearly but diplomatically, using understatement and precise word choice.

speaking_scenarios.title: An anecdote with irony
speaking_scenarios.setting: Friends swap stories about travel disasters.
speaking_scenarios.task: Tell a story with humour, irony and a well-timed understatement.

speaking_scenarios.title: Media interview
speaking_scenarios.setting: A journalist asks you about a sensitive topic in your field.
speaking_scenarios.task: Answer precisely, avoid being misquoted and resolve an ambiguous question.

sub_bands.goal: Can communicate with native-like rhetoric and sociolinguistic tact in any setting.

grammar_targets.title: Rhetorical devices: tricolon, parallelism, rhetorical questions
grammar_targets.explanation: Strengthen persuasion with groups of three, parallel structures and rhetorical questions.
grammar_targets.example: We came to listen, to learn and to lead. Why settle for less?

grammar_targets.title: Register shifting within discourse
grammar_targets.explanation: Shift deliberately between formal and informal register within one conversation, depending on the listener.
grammar_targets.example: Formally, the results are 'encouraging'. Between us? We nailed it.

grammar_targets.title: Advanced politeness and hedging strategies
grammar_targets.explanation: Protect the listener's face: I wonder whether..., It might be worth considering..., With all due respect...
grammar_targets.example: It might be worth revisiting the timeline, if that's not too disruptive.

grammar_targets.title: Discourse reference and substitution
grammar_targets.explanation: Keep text cohesive without repetition using this/that/such, do so, and the former/the latter.
grammar_targets.example: Some argued for delay; others opposed doing so. The latter prevailed.

items.example: Her speech galvanised the team.
The message resonated with young voters.
The results underscore the need for change.

items.meaning: at risk; to be won or lost
items.example: Our reputation is at stake.

items.meaning: an appeal urging people to act
items.example: End with a clear call to action.
She told a compelling story.
With all due respect, I see it differently.
I take your point, but timing matters.
If I may, I'd like to add one thing.

items.meaning: to sense the mood of a group
items.example: Good speakers read the room.
We need to tread carefully here.
Let him save face in front of the team.

can_do_statements.text: Can deliver persuasive talks with native-like rhetoric.
Can handle sensitive conversations with sociolinguistic tact.
Can write persuasive opinion pieces with a clear rhetorical structure.
Can mediate complex texts for different audiences.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: You must do this by Friday.
l1_interference_alerts.right: Would it be possible to have this by Friday?
l1_interference_alerts.note: A direct obligation that sounds neutral in Turkish can feel pushy in English.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: With all respect...
l1_interference_alerts.right: With all due respect...
l1_interference_alerts.note: The fixed phrase is 'with all due respect'.

l1_interference_alerts.wrong: (Long ceremonial introduction before the main point)
l1_interference_alerts.right: State the point early, then support it.
l1_interference_alerts.note: English rhetoric states the main point early; long introductions lose attention.

speaking_scenarios.title: Keynote opening
speaking_scenarios.setting: You open a conference with a three-minute keynote.
speaking_scenarios.task: Hook the audience, use a tricolon and a rhetorical question, and end with a call to action.

speaking_scenarios.title: Mediating a conflict
speaking_scenarios.setting: Two colleagues are in open conflict and you mediate.
speaking_scenarios.task: Acknowledge both sides, protect each person's face and steer them to an agreement.

speaking_scenarios.title: High-stakes negotiation
speaking_scenarios.setting: You negotiate a partnership with a much larger company.
speaking_scenarios.task: Hold your position, concede strategically and shift register when the tone changes.
